newsitem.title: USA: Texas teens battle school ban on rosaries.
newsitem.headline: Texas teens battle school ban on rosaries.

text.p: Two Texas high school students have found themselves at the centre of a lawsuit challenging rules banning students from wearing rosary beads around their necks because they are considered "gang apparel" by school officials.

The case, which opened Tuesday, weighs the students' religious and free-speech rights against administrators' attempts to thwart suspected gang activity in the rural New Caney school district, about 30 miles north of Houston.
"It makes me feel closer to God," David Chalifoux, a 15-year old altar boy, said of his decision to wear a rosary to school. "If I see it, it will remind me to stay out of trouble."
School officials differ, and in March Chalifoux was hauled into the principal's office by campus police officers after he was spotted wearing his pale green, glow-in-the-dark rosary in the lunchroom.

He was ordered to tuck the rosary into his shirt while at school because the beads, traditionally used in prayer and meditation by Roman Catholics, could identify wearers as gang members, school officials said.

Chalifoux and his friend, Jerry Robertson, were the only New Caney High School students openly wearing the distinctive rosaries, but officials said they were concerned the two could face retaliation from members of at least one local gang, United Homies, which adopted rosary beads as part of its gang colours.

New Caney students have been banned from wearing baggy pants, bandanas and other clothing used to identify gang members, but Chalifoux said the school did not maintain a list of forbidden items and never identified rosaries as gang apparel.

The teenagers and their parents have asked U.S. District Court Judge David Hittner for a permanent injunction against the rosary ban, along with damages and attorneys' fees. A ruling is expected before school starts next month.
